edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SCIENCE & TECH + SPORT
edition.deck: From deadly drone strikes and a Ukraine-US meeting in Oslo to a Covid inquiry report and fresh Danish economic forecasts.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and fresh reporting from the day, while avoiding repeat coverage of stories already prominent in the morning edition without a meaningful new development.

content.headline: Sudan drone strikes reportedly kill more than 200, including mourners
content.shortHeadline: Sudan drone strikes kill more than 200, sources say
content.standfirst: Reports describe strikes on a funeral convoy and markets in Sudan and the disputed Abyei region. The army is accused of carrying out attacks; the full toll and responsibility for some strikes remain unclear.

image.caption: Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei has treated people wounded in the market attack.

sources.originalTitle: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 200 people, sources say

segments.body: Drone strikes in West Kordofan reportedly killed 150 people on Sunday evening, including mourners travelling to a funeral, according to the Sudan War Observatory. In Abyei, 73 people were reported killed when a market was hit on Monday, the region’s information minister said.

segments.title: Attribution remains contested
segments.body: A military source told the BBC that Sudan’s army carried out the Abyei strike, saying the market supplied fuel to the Rapid Support Forces. The army has not responded to allegations about the West Kordofan strikes, but says it does not target civilians. South Sudan has summoned Sudan’s ambassador over the Abyei attack, amid fears of cross-border escalation.

segments.title: A widening humanitarian emergency
segments.body: The United Nations says armed drone attacks are killing civilians and disrupting essential services. The conflict has displaced more than 14 million people, while 20 million face acute hunger and famine risks are rising in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan.

content.headline: Zelensky and US envoy meet in Oslo amid dispute over intelligence
content.shortHeadline: Zelensky meets US envoy in Oslo amid intelligence dispute
content.standfirst: The talks, requested by Ukraine and hosted by Norway and Finland, come as Kyiv says unreliable US warnings are costing lives. Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejects the accusation that Washington is withholding intelligence.

image.caption: US envoy Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky meet in Oslo.

sources.originalTitle: Zelensky and US envoys holding Oslo talks as Rubio denies withholding intelligence

segments.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is meeting US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, with Jared Kushner joining by video link. Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said the talks were requested by Zelensky and come at a critical time for Ukraine.

segments.title: Disagreement over US support
segments.body: Zelensky’s military adviser Serhii Beskrestnov told the BBC that Kyiv does not always receive reliable warnings of attacks, including ballistic-missile launches. Rubio called claims that the US was withholding intelligence “scandalous”; he said nothing had been intentionally denied, though he acknowledged some Patriot interceptor missiles might not yet have arrived.

segments.title: A fraught diplomatic moment
segments.body: Relations have deteriorated after Donald Trump said Ukraine should have someone else negotiate on its behalf. Støre said the aim of the Oslo talks was to put relations on a more constructive path and work towards a lasting, just peace. It is not yet clear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia.

content.headline: Alberta voters reject move towards independence by wide margin
content.shortHeadline: Alberta voters reject independence referendum by wide margin
content.standfirst: More than two-thirds of voters backed remaining in Canada in a ballot on whether to begin the process for a binding separation referendum. Separatist leaders say their campaign will continue, leaving divisions over Alberta’s future unresolved.

image.caption: A pro-separation watch party follows the Alberta ballot results.

sources.originalTitle: Alberta votes overwhelmingly to remain part of Canada, projections suggest
Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat

segments.body: With most votes counted, more than two-thirds of Albertans had voted to remain part of Canada rather than pursue a binding referendum on separation, projected results suggest. The ballot asked whether the provincial government should begin the legal process required to hold such a referendum; it was not itself a vote on independence.

segments.title: A political test for Danielle Smith
segments.body: Prime Minister Mark Carney called the result a “clear choice”. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who supported unity but allowed the ballot to go ahead, said voters had chosen a stronger Alberta within Canada. A judge had blocked the original separation petition because it did not consult Indigenous First Nations whose land could be affected.

segments.title: Separatists vow to continue
segments.body: Separatist leaders say they will keep campaigning, and some have indicated they want to replace Smith with a leader more sympathetic to their cause. The ballot also included nine questions about greater provincial autonomy, whose preliminary results could add to debate over Alberta’s relationship with Ottawa.

content.headline: Water warning after 408 fall ill near South Africa’s capital
content.shortHeadline: 408 fall ill after contaminated water near Pretoria
content.standfirst: Most of those affected are children under four, officials say. Residents in five townships have been told not to drink or cook with tap water after testing found several pathogens in supplies from a local treatment facility.

image.caption: Water supplied to communities near Pretoria was found to contain pathogens.

sources.originalTitle: Residents warned not to drink tap water after hundreds fall sick near South Africa capital

segments.body: Authorities have detected 408 cases of illness between 7 and 18 October in townships in Tshwane, the area that includes Pretoria. Patients reported stomach cramps and diarrhoea; most were children under four. Tests found E. coli and other pathogens in water supplied by a local treatment facility.

segments.title: Residents told to avoid tap water
segments.body: Officials have declared the water unfit for human consumption and told residents to use it only for flushing toilets. Water tankers have been sent to provide clean drinking water. Authorities also advised people to discard stored water and disinfect containers with household bleach.

content.headline: Yemeni families flee renewed fighting across Red Sea to Djibouti
content.shortHeadline: Thousands of Yemenis flee fighting across the Red Sea
content.standfirst: With overland routes blocked by fighting, thousands have taken boats to Djibouti, arriving at an already stretched humanitarian site. The latest flight comes amid a sharp escalation in Yemen’s conflict and an existing aid crisis.

sources.originalTitle: Fleeing the frontline: Yemeni families cross Red Sea to Djibouti as Houthi conflict rages

segments.body: Several thousand Yemenis have fled renewed fighting for Djibouti in recent weeks, crossing the Bab al-Mandab strait by boat after safer overland routes were cut off. One father told the Guardian he took his family from a village near Mocha after fighting reached the area and government forces withdrew.

segments.title: Pressure on refuge and aid
segments.body: The latest arrivals are sheltering at the Markazi site near Obock, where capacity for shelter, water, sanitation, food and healthcare is under strain. As of 8 October, Djibouti had recorded 3,807 new Yemeni arrivals, according to Yemen’s office for assistance to refugees and disaster victims.

segments.title: A broader escalation
segments.body: The reporting says more than 900 people have been killed and at least 250,000 displaced since the renewed fighting began in August. The UN estimates that more than half of Yemen’s population needs humanitarian assistance.

content.headline: Israel’s first-time voters could help decide a tight election
content.shortHeadline: Young first-time voters could sway Israel’s close election
content.standfirst: More than half a million young people are expected to vote next week, and polls suggest many lean to the right. The reporting finds a generation divided over security, identity and the role of far-right parties.

image.caption: Itamar Ben-Gvir campaigns among young supporters in Israel.

sources.originalTitle: Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters

segments.body: More than half a million people will vote for the first time in Israel’s election next week. One newspaper poll cited by the BBC found that more than 16% of first-time voters planned to support far-right parties, while a separate Channel 12 survey found almost three-quarters described themselves as right or centre-right.

segments.title: Security and political identity
segments.body: Young supporters of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir told the BBC they associate him with strength and security, particularly after the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023. His positions include annexing the occupied West Bank and settling Gaza; these are widely condemned by liberal Israelis, and several Western countries have imposed sanctions or travel bans on him and his ally Bezalel Smotrich.

segments.title: A divided generation
segments.body: Political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin said young Israeli Jews had been more right-wing than average for about 20 years, growing up amid wars and without personal experience of peace efforts. The reporting also describes young voters backing opposition candidates and says turnout among first-time voters could matter in a close race.

content.headline: US economy grows, but tariffs and war raise costs for households
content.shortHeadline: US growth holds up as tariffs and war push up household costs
content.standfirst: The economy is growing faster than other G7 members over the period assessed, but inflation is above the rate President Donald Trump inherited and hiring has slowed. The report also finds uneven effects across household incomes.

sources.originalTitle: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?

segments.body: US GDP is expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%, and has grown about 3.2% since the end of 2024, according to the latest figures in BBC Verify’s analysis. The report says the economy has proved more resilient than many expected after Trump’s tariffs, with investment in artificial intelligence also supporting growth.

segments.title: Inflation and jobs tell a less comfortable story
segments.body: Inflation is 3.7%, up from the 3% rate Trump inherited in January 2025, and economists estimate it would have been lower without the new tariffs. The report also links higher energy prices to the Iran war. An average of 34,000 jobs a month has been added since Trump returned to office, compared with 122,000 a month in Biden’s final year.

segments.title: Uneven effects
segments.body: Median household income rose 2.6% in 2025 after adjusting for inflation. But estimates from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy suggest middle-income households are about $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would otherwise have been, while the poorest fifth are about $750 worse off; the richest 1% are estimated to be $12,560 better off, mainly because of tax cuts.

content.headline: Morocco’s first female prime minister faces a test on women’s rights
content.shortHeadline: Morocco’s first female PM faces test over women’s rights
content.standfirst: Fatima Zahra El Mansouri’s appointment is historic, but the pace of reform remains uncertain. Women’s rights advocates point to family-law changes, education and the limits of the prime minister’s power as key tests.

image.caption: Fatima Zahra El Mansouri, Morocco’s first female prime minister, with King Mohammed VI.

sources.originalTitle: Morocco's first female prime minister caught between the king, clerics, and feminists

segments.body: Morocco’s King Mohammed VI has appointed Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country’s first female prime minister. Her party won the most seats in September’s parliamentary election and has formed a coalition with three others, holding 207 of 395 seats.

segments.title: A role with limits
segments.body: The appointment has exposed continuing reservations about women in senior positions, while the king retains extensive powers, including over defence and foreign affairs. Reforms to the family code announced in 2024 have not become law; debates include inheritance, polygamy, marriage, divorce and child custody.

segments.title: What advocates want to see
segments.body: Women’s rights advocate Yasmina Benslimane called the appointment a barrier-breaking moment but said El Mansouri’s actions would matter more than her gender. The report also describes demands for better support for girls’ education, particularly in rural areas, and notes that El Mansouri has not said whether she will advance family-code reforms.

content.headline: Covid inquiry finds care homes were left dangerously exposed
content.shortHeadline: Covid inquiry finds care homes were left dangerously exposed
content.standfirst: The inquiry says failures to advise isolation for patients discharged from hospital helped the virus spread in care homes. Its chair also describes the emotional harm caused by restrictions on visits to dying relatives.

image.caption: The Covid inquiry report covers deaths in UK care homes during the pandemic.

sources.originalTitle: UK government failures led to Covid spreading ‘like wildfire’ in care homes, inquiry finds

segments.body: The Covid inquiry has found that adult social care was treated as “something of an afterthought” during the pandemic. Chair Heather Hallett said the government’s failure to advise care homes to isolate patients discharged from hospital was a significant omission that created conditions in which the virus spread rapidly.

segments.title: Death, isolation and accountability
segments.body: More than 43,000 people died from Covid-19 in UK care homes between March 2020 and July 2022. Hallett said bans on visits caused immense emotional harm and left residents isolated; she rejected former health secretary Matt Hancock’s claim that he had thrown a “protective ring” around care homes.

segments.title: Recommendations for the next pandemic
segments.body: The report recommends stronger pandemic planning, financial support for social-care staff to self-isolate, guidance on visiting restrictions and better inspection during lockdowns. It also calls the lack of protective equipment for care-home staff “wholly unacceptable” and urges the recommendations to be acted on before another pandemic.

content.headline: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra set to close
content.shortHeadline: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra to close
content.standfirst: BBC Three and BBC Scotland will become online-only, while Radio 4 Extra will close, as the corporation seeks £500m in savings. The announcement leaves questions about broadcast services and further cuts still to come.

image.caption: BBC Three launched programmes including Fleabag and Killing Eve.

sources.originalTitle: BBC Three and BBC Scotland TV channels to be shut down next year
BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra broadcast channels to close

segments.body: The BBC says BBC Three and BBC Scotland will stop broadcasting on television in the spring and become online-only; Radio 4 Extra will also close. The corporation says much of the TV channels’ content will remain on iPlayer, while Radio 4 Extra’s archive programming is largely available on BBC Sounds.

segments.title: More savings may follow
segments.body: The closures form part of a £500m savings drive. The Guardian reports that only about £200m has been cut so far, leaving further difficult decisions ahead. BBC Scotland’s nightly Reporting Scotland: News at Seven will end with the channel and will not move to iPlayer, the BBC says.

segments.title: Questions over public-service output
segments.body: The BBC says it must adapt to audiences increasingly watching on demand. The Guardian reports concern among some staff that cuts could target programming commercial rivals would not provide, while the union Equity said the announcement did not signal a thriving BBC and raised concerns about its ability to meet its duties.

content.headline: Google cloud outage disrupts UK courts and banking services
content.shortHeadline: Google cloud outage disrupts courts and UK banking
content.standfirst: A power problem at Google’s London cloud operations disrupted remote court hearings and banking services before most affected services were restored. The incident is an early test of new regulatory powers over critical cloud providers.

image.caption: The Google cloud outage disrupted services including Revolut’s app.

sources.originalTitle: Google cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offline

segments.body: A power event affecting Google’s London-based cloud operations disrupted services across the UK on Tuesday. The remote-hearing system used by courts in England and Wales failed during the morning, delaying several hearings, while customers of Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut reported problems with banking services.

segments.title: Services return, with questions outstanding
segments.body: Google said services were coming back online from about 1pm London time and were restored for most customers by 3pm. Disruptions included card payments, transfers and cash withdrawals. Revolut said customers’ money and data were safe; Google said it would publish an analysis after its investigation.

segments.title: A regulatory test
segments.body: The Financial Conduct Authority said it was in contact with Google and seeking more information. The outage is the first major test of powers recently given to the FCA and Bank of England to regulate Google and other providers supplying critical cloud services to UK financial firms.

content.headline: Storm Austen to bring strong winds to southern UK on Friday
content.shortHeadline: Storm Austen could bring winds above 70mph to exposed coasts
content.standfirst: The Met Office has issued a yellow wind warning for parts of south-west England and southern Wales, with gusts of 50–60mph more widely and stronger winds possible on exposed coasts. The storm’s precise track is still being assessed.

sources.originalTitle: Storm Austen forecast to hit southern UK

segments.body: Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season, is expected to approach south-west England on Thursday and move west to east on Friday. A yellow wind warning covers much of south-west England and southern Wales from midnight to midday on Friday, with parts of the south coast also affected.

segments.title: Forecast still developing
segments.body: The Met Office says gusts of 50–60mph are likely across much of the warning area and could exceed 70mph on the most exposed coasts. The storm’s exact track and position are still being determined; rain and further unsettled weather are also forecast later in the week and into the weekend.

content.headline: Tommy Robinson threatened journalist’s family, court is told
content.shortHeadline: Court hears Tommy Robinson threatened journalist’s family
content.standfirst: A MailOnline journalist told the court he feared for his family after an alleged menacing call and the online publication of his address. Robinson denies two harassment charges; the claims are being heard at trial.

image.caption: Tommy Robinson outside Southwark Crown Court on Tuesday.

sources.originalTitle: Tommy Robinson threatened to publish details about journalist’s family, court told

segments.body: A court has heard that Tommy Robinson allegedly threatened to publish details about a journalist’s family and warned they would have to move home. Andrew Young said he feared that Robinson’s followers could target him or his family after his home address appeared on X.

segments.title: Charges denied
segments.body: Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, denies two counts of harassment causing fear of violence against MailOnline journalists Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. The charges relate to alleged conduct in 2024. The court also heard that unknown men appeared outside journalists’ homes and that Dirnhuber said he had to leave his address.

content.headline: Silicosis compensation for bereaved kitchen workers’ families set to rise
content.shortHeadline: Silicosis compensation for bereaved families set to rise
content.standfirst: Draft rules would increase payments to families of workers who die from industrial lung disease, including silicosis. The change follows a campaign on engineered-stone dust, but remains subject to parliamentary approval.

image.caption: Sandra Elliott’s husband died from silicosis after working with stone.

sources.originalTitle: Families of kitchen workers killed by toxic dust set to get thousands in compensation
Revealed: The human cost of UK’s killer kitchens – with 166 firms breaking law

segments.body: New regulations due for parliamentary consideration would increase compensation for families of workers who die from industrial lung diseases. Bereaved families have received an average of £10,700, compared with £17,700 for sick workers, according to The i Paper; the change is intended to address that gap.

segments.title: A continuing workplace risk
segments.body: The proposed rules apply to diseases including pneumoconiosis, which can be caused by silica dust released when engineered stone is cut. Almost 60 UK workers have been diagnosed with silicosis so far, though doctors believe the true number is higher. The regulations are due to take effect on 31 October if approved by Parliament.

segments.title: Safety enforcement
segments.body: The i Paper reports that, of 434 engineered-stone businesses inspected by the Health and Safety Executive, 166 received legally binding enforcement notices. The HSE has issued guidance against dry-cutting engineered stone without water suppression, but inspectors have found firms still using unsafe practices.

content.headline: Aberfan remembers 1966 disaster as coal-tip risks remain
content.shortHeadline: Aberfan marks 60 years as coal-tip safety concerns persist
content.standfirst: Survivors and families are preparing to mark the disaster’s 60th anniversary on Wednesday. As the community works to preserve its memory, thousands of disused coal tips in Wales remain a safety concern and remediation is expected to cost more than pledged funding.

image.caption: The Aberfan disaster killed more than 100 children when coal waste struck Pantglas school.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I survived for a reason’: Aberfan fights to preserve memory of disaster 60 years on

segments.body: Aberfan survivor David Davies was eight when a coal tip collapsed onto Pantglas school, killing 116 children and 28 adults. He is helping organise the village’s 60th-anniversary remembrance on 21 October, as survivors consider how to keep the disaster in public memory.

segments.title: Memory and unfinished justice
segments.body: New exhibitions, a requiem and a national tour of a play will mark the anniversary. The report recalls that a 1967 tribunal blamed the National Coal Board, but no directors or employees were prosecuted. Families received little compensation, and money was taken from a charitable disaster fund to clear tips above the village.

segments.title: A continuing safety challenge
segments.body: The Guardian reports that about 2,000 disused coal tips in the South Wales valleys still pose safety and environmental risks. Governments have pledged £220m for maintenance and remediation, while the estimated cost of making the tips safe exceeds £600m.

content.headline: RSPCA warns of cat rescue capacity crisis as arrivals rise
content.shortHeadline: RSPCA says cat arrivals are outpacing rehoming
content.standfirst: The charity says it is running out of space as cats and kittens arrive faster than they can be rehomed. It is urging people to consider adopting or fostering, while pointing to rising cases involving many animals at one address.

image.caption: The RSPCA is asking prospective pet owners to consider adopting cats.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We really need help’: RSPCA faces capacity crisis as cats arrive faster than they can be rehomed

segments.body: The RSPCA says cats now outnumber dogs in its shelters and are arriving faster than they can be rehomed. It looked after 6,408 cats in its 14 animal centres last year and had taken in 5,616 by October this year; across its wider care network, about 20,000 cats were taken in during 2025.

segments.title: Pressure on rescue services
segments.body: The charity says it responded to 1,780 incidents involving 10 or more cats at one address in 2025, involving more than 36,000 cats. It is asking prospective pet owners to consider adopting adult cats and is seeking more foster carers as it faces a shortage of space.

content.headline: EU Arctic plan proposes more icebreakers and a new Greenland cable
content.shortHeadline: EU Arctic strategy proposes icebreakers and Greenland cable
content.standfirst: The European Commission’s new strategy focuses on security, infrastructure and countering disinformation. It proposes joint icebreaker purchases but gives no numbers, budget or timetable for the plan.

image.caption: Finland’s icebreaker Kontio in Arctic waters.

sources.originalTitle: Efter Grønland-aftale: Flere isbrydere skal sikre kritisk infrastruktur

segments.body: The European Commission wants to strengthen security in Arctic waters, including by exploring joint purchases of icebreakers by EU members and partner countries. It says the vessels could help in crises, including efforts to repair undersea cables. The strategy sets no target for how many icebreakers to acquire, or when and at what cost.

segments.title: Greenland’s place in the plan
segments.body: The Commission also wants to strengthen digital links between Greenland and Europe through a proposed undersea cable connecting Europe with Japan via Greenland and Canada. The EU has already invested €107m in improving digital infrastructure between Europe and the Arctic, according to DR.

segments.title: Disinformation and security
segments.body: The strategy also sets out work with Arctic organisations and social-media platforms to identify disinformation. The Commission points to Russian military activity and sabotage attempts in the region; Denmark currently has no icebreakers, while EU countries together have about 10.

content.headline: Danish economic council forecasts slower growth after strong year
content.shortHeadline: Danish growth forecast to slow after pharma-driven surge
content.standfirst: The Economic Councils expect growth to ease from 4.2% this year to 1.8% in 2027 and 1.3% in 2028 as the exceptional boost from pharmaceuticals fades. A higher-energy-price scenario would bring greater inflation and weaker employment growth.

sources.originalTitle: Markant lavere vækst i dansk økonomi, forudser vismænd

segments.body: Denmark’s GDP is forecast to grow 4.2% this year, then 1.8% in 2027 and 1.3% in 2028, according to the Economic Councils’ autumn report. The strong performance this year is driven in particular by pharmaceuticals; the councils expect that exceptional contribution to end in coming years.

segments.title: The risk from energy prices
segments.body: The main forecast assumes energy prices gradually fall. In a risk scenario based on an OECD report, oil costs an average of $102 a barrel in both 2027 and 2028. The councils say that would raise inflation and weaken international growth, creating a serious external shock for Denmark.

segments.title: Different outlook for jobs and prices
segments.body: In the main forecast, inflation is expected to be 2.1% in 2027 and employment to rise by 16,000. Under the higher-energy-price scenario, inflation reaches 3.2% and employment growth is 4,000, according to the report.

content.headline: Former top lawyer says he should have alerted police about alleged invoice fraud
content.shortHeadline: Former lawyer says he should have alerted police over invoice-fraud ‘h
content.standfirst: Nicolai Dyhr told a court he should have informed police after hearing an allegation of a possible “invoice factory” in companies whose insolvencies he handled. He denies charges of abuse of office and giving false information.

image.caption: Nicolai Dyhr during the TV 2 documentary The Black Swan.

sources.originalTitle: Håndskrevet note belaster tidligere topadvokat: 'Jeg sad med munden fuld af wienerbrød'
Han var prominent topadvokat: Men så satte tv-program en lavine i gang

segments.body: Former insolvency lawyer Nicolai Dyhr told a court that he should have alerted police after hearing information about a possible “invoice factory” at a meeting in January 2023. He said he did not believe money laundering had taken place in the two companies, but accepted that failing to pass on the information was his mistake.

segments.title: Evidence from hidden recordings
segments.body: Prosecutors played recordings from TV 2’s documentary The Black Swan, including a 2022 meeting in which Dyhr discussed unexplained invoices and a possible bankruptcy case. He called one of his recorded remarks “stupid” and said he had not understood its seriousness. Dyhr denies the charges of abuse of office and giving false information.

segments.title: The case against him
segments.body: The prosecution alleges that Dyhr failed to adequately inform the bankruptcy court about information concerning businessman Martin Malm’s companies. Malm is separately charged with aggravated money laundering and tax fraud involving more than 23 million kroner; he denies those charges, according to DR.

content.headline: Survey: half of Danish public-school teachers feel stressed weekly or daily
content.shortHeadline: Half of Danish public-school teachers report weekly stress
content.standfirst: In a survey of 1,901 teachers and early-grade leaders, 52% said they feel stressed at work daily or weekly. Respondents most often cited workload, classroom disruption and insufficient time or support.

sources.originalTitle: For lidt tid og for meget uro får lærere til at føle sig stressede

segments.body: A Danish Teachers’ Association survey found that 16% of respondents felt stressed at work daily and 36% weekly. The survey was answered by 1,901 public-school teachers and early-grade leaders; nine in 10 of those reporting stress attributed it to work-related conditions.

segments.title: Workload and support cited
segments.body: Respondents described too little preparation time, classroom disruption and difficulty getting support for pupils with additional needs. More than a third said they had at some point taken sick leave because of stress, according to the association.

segments.title: Calls for changes
segments.body: The association’s president says staff shortages and teachers leaving the profession make the findings a school-workplace problem. A researcher on teacher stress said delays in getting help for pupils can leave teachers responsible without the authority to resolve the problem. Teachers most often identified fewer teaching hours, better pupil support and more preparation time as potential measures.

content.headline: Former MP sent nearly 1,200 questions on sewage overflows before exit
content.shortHeadline: Former MP sent nearly 1,200 sewage-overflow questions
content.standfirst: Søren Gade sent the Environment Ministry questions covering all 98 municipalities four days before announcing his departure from parliament. The ministry says answering them will require substantial work from officials.

image.caption: Venstre politician Søren Gade announced he was leaving parliament.

sources.originalTitle: Før sit exit sendte Søren Gade en regulær spørgsmålsstorm mod miljøministeren

segments.body: Four days before announcing he would leave parliament, Venstre politician Søren Gade submitted nearly 1,200 written questions to the environment minister. The questions repeat 12 topics for each of Denmark’s 98 municipalities, focusing on how sewage overflows are recorded and what authorities know about them.

segments.title: Ministry says responses will take time
segments.body: The ministry described the volume of questions from a single MP on the same day as unusual and said it would need input from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency. It expects the answers to require considerable resources from both the agency and ministry.

segments.title: A dispute over the figures
segments.body: Bæredygtigt Landbrug welcomed the questions, saying answers could clarify what reaches waterways. Some in agriculture suspect sewage overflows are not recorded accurately, but the report presents this as a dispute over the data, not established evidence of incorrect reporting.

content.headline: Blind Danes say quiet electric vehicles make traffic less safe
content.shortHeadline: Blind pedestrians warn of risks from quiet electric vehicles
content.standfirst: A blind man in Broager says an electric car ran over his foot, while the Danish Association of the Blind reports that quiet vehicles are a major source of insecurity. The available crossing signals remain limited, according to the association.

sources.originalTitle: Elbiler gør trafikken utryg for blinde: - Pludselig blev min fod kørt over

segments.body: Stig Hansen, who is blind, says a slowly moving electric car ran over his foot at a crossing in Broager. He says some electric vehicles are difficult to hear at low speed, despite EU rules requiring new electric cars to emit an artificial warning sound at low speeds.

segments.title: Access to audible crossing signals
segments.body: The Danish Association of the Blind says electric cars, e-bikes and e-scooters make traffic less safe for blind and partially sighted people. Its 2024 survey found quiet vehicles were their leading concern; the association says only 15% of crossings in Denmark have audible signals or other sound cues.

segments.title: Local infrastructure constraints
segments.body: Sønderborg Municipality says audible signals are installed at about 20% of its signal-controlled junctions. It says adding them to older crossings can require substantial construction work and funding that has not been allocated for every location.

content.headline: Copenhagen mayor says care homes can serve beef despite food guidance
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen mayor says care homes may serve beef
content.standfirst: A dispute over birthday meals at care homes has exposed different readings of Copenhagen’s food guidance. The mayor says it does not ban beef, while the health and care mayor says staff treat it as a requirement and wants older people exempted.

image.caption: Copenhagen health and care mayor Jens Kristian Lütken wants older people exempted from the city’s food strategy.

sources.originalTitle: Overborgmester slår fast: Server den hakkebøf

segments.body: Copenhagen’s lord mayor, Sisse Marie Welling, says the city’s food strategy does not prevent care homes from serving beef, including minced-beef patties. She says the guidance focuses more on nutrition than climate and is not mandatory.

segments.title: Officials disagree over how it works in practice
segments.body: Health and care mayor Jens Kristian Lütken says the guidance is too rigid and that care homes take it seriously as a requirement. He wants the strategy changed so the older-persons sector is exempt. The debate follows an analysis describing cases where residents’ requests for beef were reportedly refused over emissions concerns.

content.headline: Danish researchers test fermentation to improve fava bean flavour
content.shortHeadline: Fermentation could make fava beans more appealing, study finds
content.standfirst: A University of Copenhagen study found fermentation changed flavour compounds in fava-bean protein, reducing characteristic bean notes and producing nutty and umami aromas. The researchers have not yet tested how people perceive the taste.

image.caption: Fava beans are being studied as a source of plant protein.

sources.originalTitle: Bønner smager for meget af bønner: Nu vil forskere gøre noget ved det

segments.body: Researchers at the University of Copenhagen tested fermenting fava-bean protein extracts with different bacteria. Their analysis found the process could reduce the beans’ characteristic flavour and produce other aromas, including nutty and umami notes.

segments.title: Potential food and farming uses
segments.body: The researchers say the approach could help develop plant-based alternatives to meat. Fava beans can grow in Danish conditions and may replace some imported soy in animal feed; legumes can also take nitrogen from the air, reducing the need for nitrogen fertiliser.

segments.title: Early-stage research
segments.body: The study measured changes in aroma compounds, not people’s responses to the taste. The researchers say further work is needed before the results can translate into products on supermarket shelves.

content.headline: Kiran Leonard finds a path beyond the teenage-prodigy label
content.shortHeadline: Kiran Leonard moves beyond the prodigy years
content.standfirst: Once patronised for his precocious, densely composed music, the Saddleworth-born artist describes leaving his first industry team and finding a new creative community in London.

image.caption: Kiran Leonard, experimental musician and songwriter.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I had no plan. Just total scorched earth’: how Kiran Leonard survived teen success to make songs of full-body joy

segments.body: Kiran Leonard was hailed as a prodigy at 16, but says early coverage fetishised the ambition and complexity of his music in ways that felt patronising. After releasing four albums, he ditched his management team without a plan and struggled to find gigs or a new manager.

segments.title: Finding a different voice
segments.body: Leonard gradually found his footing through shows and friendships with musicians including Caroline. He now sees his work as a series of distinct investigations, and says he is drawn less to stylistic labels than to sounds that create a physical feeling. Much of his work remains solitary, with collaborations offering a different voice.

content.headline: Brazilian pop fandoms mobilise online for Lula ahead of the runoff
content.shortHeadline: Brazilian pop fans campaign for Lula
content.standfirst: More than 600 fan groups have joined a digital campaign backing Brazil’s president in the 25 October runoff. Their organisers see fan communities as a way to bring political debate to people who may not follow it elsewhere.

image.caption: Two pop fans at a pro-Lula demonstration in São Paulo.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Taylor Swift tells us to take the lead!’ Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?

segments.body: After the first round of Brazil’s presidential election, more than 600 fan groups for international and Brazilian pop artists joined Fandoms Pelo Brasil, an online campaign supporting Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro is scheduled for 25 October. The campaign grew from fan accounts offering Lula’s team access to their social media audiences.

perspectives.body: Organisers say fan accounts can carry political discussion to people who follow artists and fan communities but do not keep up with politics. The reporting also notes the limits: some Brazilian fan groups back Bolsonaro, while Shakira’s team has restricted political use of her image.

segments.title: Fandom becomes a campaign network
segments.body: The effort has moved from online posts to street organising, with pop-culture symbols appearing at a Lula rally in São Paulo. The government has also courted fans through measures such as a decree targeting ticket-scalping bots and requiring free drinking water at large public events. The groups’ support is not presented as universal, but their mobilisation has become part of the runoff campaign.

content.headline: Ed Sanders reflects on the Fugs and a life of countercultural protest
content.shortHeadline: Ed Sanders on the Fugs and a life of protest
content.standfirst: The 87-year-old musician, poet and activist speaks as a documentary about the Fugs reaches UK audiences, revisiting the band’s anti-war theatrics, battles over censorship and eclectic music.

image.caption: Ed Sanders, right, with Fugs bandmate Tuli Kupferberg.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We tried to levitate the Pentagon’: the almost unbelievable life of Ed Sanders, trickster god of the US counterculture

segments.body: Ed Sanders led the Fugs, whose mix of poetry, folk, garage rock and theatrical provocation made them part of New York’s 1960s counterculture. Speaking as the documentary Fugs Film! receives its UK premiere, Sanders recalls the band’s aim to protest the American war machine as well as make music.

perspectives.body: Sanders says the group’s plan to “levitate” the Pentagon was a deliberately absurd spectacle designed to focus attention on an anti-war protest. He describes that activism as a continuing struggle, not a victory secured in the 1960s.

segments.title: Art, provocation and the cost of refusing to compromise
segments.body: The band’s provocations brought censorship battles and, Sanders says, helped cost them an Atlantic Records release after he refused to remove an offensive song. He now sees some of the group’s songs differently, but argues that music and protest belonged together in the Fugs’ work.

content.headline: The Avalanches turn advertising jingles into a bittersweet sound collage
content.shortHeadline: The Avalanches make a collage of commercial noise
content.standfirst: No Bad Memories folds advertising voices and audio logos into the Australian group’s sample-rich pop. The review hears an exuberant, sprawling record shadowed by the fading shared references of mass media.

sources.originalTitle: No Bad Memories

segments.body: On No Bad Memories, the Avalanches build a continuous, 52-minute collage from decades of advertising jingles, audio logos and spoken copy, alongside vintage soul and easy listening. The interruption of a dance track by a flatly delivered “Toshiba” is both a joke and a reminder that the record’s playful sound is not outside commercial culture.

segments.title: A nostalgia without a monoculture
segments.body: The review finds the album closer to the immersive sample collage of Since I Left You than the group’s more conventional later songwriting, while noting its long track list and numerous interludes. Its deeper melancholy comes from the question of whether a sound can still summon collective nostalgia when audiences no longer share the same mass-media touchstones.

content.headline: Zach Bryan’s new EP finds focus in sobriety and a bid for adulthood
content.shortHeadline: Zach Bryan finds focus on a new EP
content.standfirst: On Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs, the country songwriter pares back his usual sprawl to examine sobriety, love and the damage of old habits. The review sees a more controlled, forward-looking record.

sources.originalTitle: Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs EP

segments.body: Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs is Zach Bryan’s first music written and recorded while sober. Across eight songs, he looks back at personal turmoil and the habits he is trying to leave behind, in a more concise and controlled set than his often sprawling albums.

segments.title: The unevenness of moving on
segments.body: The review hears his strongest writing in songs about change, including a duet with Turnpike Troubadours singer Evan Felker that links shared roots to the difficult work of breaking harmful habits. A duet with Lana Del Rey is judged less successful, but the record’s overall movement from recent mistakes towards a possible future gives it its shape.

content.headline: Way Dynamic’s Massive Shoe finds tenderness in bruised pop songs
content.shortHeadline: Way Dynamic make warm pop with a bruised edge
content.standfirst: Dylan Young’s Melbourne group draws on familiar pop sounds for gentle melodies, but the album’s strongest moments turn on rambling guitars and sharply expressed regret.

sources.originalTitle: Massive Shoe

segments.body: Way Dynamic’s third album, Massive Shoe, moves between bright, guitar-led pop and looser, more searching songs. The review hears the record’s warmth in its stacked harmonies and melodic ease, but finds its most affecting work where that lightness meets the sting of a failed relationship.

segments.title: When the regret cuts through
segments.body: “Miffed It” is singled out for its plain admission of a love mishandled, while “I Was the Dancer” opens into an unexpectedly expansive, jam-like passage. Some of the album’s more playful references and arrangements are less substantial, but the review values the tension between Young’s sunny musical surfaces and unsettled lyrics.

content.headline: Renny Conti’s Split Second renders grief as a shifting haze
content.shortHeadline: Renny Conti writes through grief’s haze
content.standfirst: Written after the death of his older brother, Split Second moves between soft, drifting arrangements and moments of startling clarity. The review finds its most powerful passages when Conti’s memories become sharply specific.

sources.originalTitle: Split Second

segments.body: Renny Conti wrote Split Second in the months after his older brother Andrew died. Its quiet voice and slow-moving arrangements evoke grief as a disorienting presence: the knowledge that someone is gone colliding with the feeling that they remain close.

segments.title: Moments that come into focus
segments.body: The review praises the album’s hazy atmosphere but sometimes longs for more detail to break through it. A direct line placing Conti in Prospect Park as he writes to escape a “death-induced funk” provides that clarity; the album is most affecting, the critic argues, when its private loss takes vivid, particular form.

content.headline: Worldpeace DMT’s Stick Around for Tea turns indie pop into a playful musical
content.shortHeadline: Worldpeace DMT make a playful indie-pop musical
content.standfirst: The London duo’s digitally assembled songs sound like a deliberately scrappy stage show, balancing schoolyard playfulness with moments of genuine ache. The review finds the apparent silliness more carefully made than it first appears.

sources.originalTitle: Stick Around for Tea

segments.body: Worldpeace DMT’s Stick Around for Tea pares back the sound collage of the duo’s debut in favour of songs that feel like scenes in a low-budget musical. Chiptuned textures, toy-like sounds and singsong vocals keep the record playful, while Rowan Please’s performance and Leo Fincham’s arrangements reveal a deliberate tension between childhood and adulthood.

segments.title: A joke with feeling underneath
segments.body: The review points to “Stratocaster” as a sparse, darkly poetic song delivered with the simplicity of a nursery rhyme, and to the title track’s engineered contrast between synthetic rhythm and a human chorus. The record repeatedly invites the question of whether its creators are serious; the critic’s answer is that the self-conscious play is part of the craft, not evidence against it.

content.headline: Michael Jackson biopic sequel may address abuse allegations from his perspective
content.shortHeadline: Michael Jackson sequel may address abuse allegations
content.standfirst: Jaafar Jackson says a second film will offer more of his uncle’s point of view. That approach follows criticism that the authorised first biopic omitted allegations and the perspectives of those who made them.

image.caption: Jaafar Jackson as Michael Jackson in the film Michael.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s important that Michael’s voice is heard’: Jaafar Jackson says second biopic of his uncle will cover sexual abuse allegations

segments.body: Jaafar Jackson, who made his screen debut playing his uncle in Michael, says a second film will give more attention to the late singer’s perspective on the sexual abuse allegations against him. The first biopic did not address the allegations; a legal clause prevented the depiction of one accuser, and a planned police-raid sequence was cut.

segments.title: A disputed account
segments.body: Jackson says the family has wanted the singer’s voice heard. Dan Reed, director of the documentary Leaving Neverland, sharply criticised the first film for distorting the subject and excluding the allegations. Jackson was accused of sexually abusing a child in 1993 and settled out of court; he was acquitted of other child sexual abuse charges in 2005. How a sequel will handle the competing accounts remains unknown.

perspectives.body: Reed says the first biopic reversed the truth by presenting Jackson without serious scrutiny and objected to its omission of the allegations. Jaafar Jackson, by contrast, says a sequel should give greater weight to his uncle’s point of view.

content.headline: Ghosts cast explain why the finished sitcom is returning as a film
content.shortHeadline: Why the Ghosts team brought the story back as a film
content.standfirst: The creators say they had no plan to revive their sitcom after its 2023 finale. A new film gave them a way to reunite the ensemble without simply stretching a television episode to feature length.

image.caption: The Ghosts cast in Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We’ll keep doing this if people pay us!’ The cast of TV hit Ghosts on making a movie – and maybe a caveman spinoff

segments.body: Ghosts ended in 2023 with its creators believing the story was complete. The cast says a film only became appealing after they found a premise—possession—that could let one of the ghosts leave Button House and create stakes suited to a feature. The result, Ghosts: The Possession of Button House, continues the story without restarting the series.

segments.title: A reunion, not a promise of more
segments.body: The team describes the production as a quick decision driven partly by missing one another after years of working together. They are cautious about promising further films, though Laurence Rickard jokes that caveman Robin could support a spin-off. The creators say there is no secret project in development.

content.headline: Sitges festival finds horror in motherhood, politics and the uncanny
content.shortHeadline: The unsettling discoveries of the Sitges film festival
content.standfirst: This year’s fantastic film festival ranged from sinister children and body horror to an Indonesian prison ghost story. The critic’s highlights include films that mix genre shocks with social unease and unexpected warmth.

image.caption: A scene from The Spiral, one of the films screened at Sitges.

sources.originalTitle: Explosive births, talking foxes and the devil in a trenchcoat – the Sitges fantastic film festival in all its creepy glory

segments.body: The 59th Sitges festival was crowded with stories of fraught motherhood, from Nightborn’s unsettling newborn to films about postpartum depression and a child who disrupts a scout troop. Marion Le Coroller’s Sanguine won best feature, while the festival also recognised performances in The Spiral and The Birthday Party.

segments.title: Standout films beyond the competition
segments.body: The critic’s favourites included a time-loop story that darkens as it unfolds, a return to J-horror in The Mouths, and Sabu’s crime comedy Arrested Memory. The strongest recommendation is Joko Anwar’s Ghost in the Cell, which layers a supernatural curse onto prison violence and a critique of Indonesian corruption while retaining an unexpectedly warmhearted tone.

content.headline: Children of the Wicker Man turns a folk-horror legacy into family history
content.shortHeadline: The family story behind The Wicker Man
content.standfirst: Robin Hardy’s sons revisit the making and afterlife of his cult film, but the documentary’s personal force comes with gaps in the family account and unanswered questions about absent voices.

image.caption: A still from Children of the Wicker Man.

sources.originalTitle: Children of the Wicker Man review – how the folk-horror classic haunted the family that made it

segments.body: Children of the Wicker Man, made by Robin Hardy’s sons Justin and Dominic, connects the troubled production of the 1973 film with its rise from box-office failure to cult status. It also becomes a personal reckoning with a father who left one son’s life, making the documentary’s family history as prominent as the film’s legacy.

segments.title: The silences in the account
segments.body: The review admires the brothers’ willingness to share painful memories but finds the film weakened by missing perspectives, including those of their siblings and other people central to the story. Justin’s anger and Dominic’s greater sympathy give the documentary distinct emotional registers, but do not resolve the absences.

content.headline: Digger’s box-office failure sharpens its bleak climate-change warning
content.shortHeadline: Digger’s flop sharpens its climate warning
content.standfirst: Tom Cruise’s misanthropic satire has been pulled from many US cinemas after a disastrous opening. The film’s critic argues that its depiction of public complicity makes it a revealing, if deeply flawed, climate story.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Cruise’s Digger is a commercial flop – but also the perfect climate film for our time

segments.body: In Digger, an oilman’s drilling triggers a vast iceberg that threatens Europe. The film has been savaged by critics and suffered a steep box-office drop; the article reports a predicted loss of $245m and says it was removed from more than 2,500 US theatres before its third week.

segments.title: A critique with its own blind spots
segments.body: The argument for the film is that it goes beyond blaming one oil executive, confronting viewers with their own dependence on fossil fuels and the reluctance to change. But the piece also notes its nihilism and its dismissal of clean energy, which undercuts the urgency of that critique. Its failure may also make studios less willing to back similarly direct climate films.

content.headline: Judi Dench calls Cats a waste of goodwill and talent
content.shortHeadline: Judi Dench reflects on the failed Cats film
content.standfirst: In a forthcoming memoir, Dench says the film’s intentions were honourable but its elements did not come together. She also describes discomfort on set and recalls the hostile response to the finished adaptation.

image.caption: Judi Dench as Old Deuteronomy in Cats.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Oh God, I can’t bear it’: Judi Dench says Cats film was ‘a waste of goodwill and talent’

segments.body: Judi Dench writes in her forthcoming memoir that the 2019 film adaptation of Cats was “a waste of all that goodwill and talent”. She says she never saw the final cut and cannot judge it herself, but understands why critics were hostile and felt ill at ease in her role as Old Deuteronomy.

segments.title: An unsuccessful production without villains
segments.body: Dench criticises how young dancers were left exhausted and ignored between takes, while also saying nobody set out to make a bad film and that the people involved had honourable intentions. Andrew Lloyd Webber has been much harsher, calling the adaptation wrong and saying the experience left him emotionally damaged.

perspectives.body: Dench describes a failed collaboration without assigning blame to individual makers. Lloyd Webber, who was not consulted in the way he expected, has repeatedly condemned the film and its treatment of the original musical.

content.headline: Hartlepool fishers turn suspected pollution into an environmental campaign
content.shortHeadline: Hartlepool fishers take their pollution concerns to film
content.standfirst: Jeanie Finlay’s documentary follows fishermen facing collapsing catches after a mass marine die-off. Their independent study finds evidence of a possible link to industrial chemicals, while officials have disputed their account.

image.caption: Hartlepool fisherman Stan Rennie in All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea.

sources.originalTitle: All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea review – stirring portrait of fishers driven to eco-activism

segments.body: After thousands of crabs, starfish and lobsters washed up dead on the northeast coast in 2021, Hartlepool fishermen suspected industrial pollution. An official investigation pointed instead to an algal bloom; unconvinced, the fishermen funded an independent study, which found evidence of a link to pyridine, a byproduct of steelmaking.

perspectives.body: The documentary follows the fishermen’s investigation and their belief that sediment dredged from the River Tees and dumped at sea may be responsible. The review reports evidence of a possible chemical link, not a settled finding of causation.

segments.title: Livelihoods and local power
segments.body: With catches down 80%, rising fuel costs and boats up for sale, the fishermen’s campaign is also a fight for their livelihoods. The film links the dispute to dredging for a Tees Valley freeport and shows the mayor dismissing the fishermen as conspiracy theorists and activists.

content.headline: Smart TVs leave some viewers worried about privacy and control
content.shortHeadline: Viewers push back against smart TV surveillance
content.standfirst: Some owners are disconnecting devices, modifying remotes or buying simpler screens to avoid unwanted updates, adverts and data collection. A report alleging LG TVs record audio has been denied by the company.

image.caption: A viewer with a smart television.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV

segments.body: Some viewers say smart TVs have become harder to use as software updates, paid-service prompts and advertising crowd out the simple functions they want. Several people interviewed keep their screens offline or use external devices, citing both reliability and privacy concerns.

perspectives.body: TV specialist Tom Parsons says cheaper sets can slow under the demands of their software, while noting that most shoppers still want an all-in-one entertainment system. That preference has left few straightforward, non-connected televisions on sale.

segments.title: The limits of opting out
segments.body: The article describes a YouTube investigation alleging that LG televisions record audio even when offline or powered down; LG denied the allegations. Some owners have responded by modifying devices, while proposed changes to broadcast services in the UK and Australia could make internet-connected viewing harder to avoid.

content.headline: Freddie Meredith goes from bar work to SNL UK in a rapid comedy ascent
content.shortHeadline: Freddie Meredith’s unlikely leap to SNL UK
content.standfirst: After waiting tables and reworking a struggling Edinburgh show, the comedian was asked to join Saturday Night Live UK at short notice. He discusses the awkward characters and observations that helped him find an audience.

image.caption: Comedian and SNL UK cast member Freddie Meredith.

sources.originalTitle: ‘They said: there’s this part … he’s an idiot!’ SNL UK’s Freddie Meredith on his unlikely route to comedy’s big leagues

segments.body: Freddie Meredith was working in a bar and preparing for his Edinburgh Fringe debut when his character show Need a Light? began to find an audience. A best newcomer nomination and a sold-out London transfer followed; just before the final Fringe performance, he was invited to join the cast of Saturday Night Live UK.

segments.title: The comedy of uncomfortable men
segments.body: Meredith’s work focuses on socially awkward men trying to fit in, drawing on jobs behind bars and small observations of people at the edge of a scene. He says his interest in men drawn to misogynistic online ideas is both comic material and a subject that needs careful handling: audiences may laugh without recognising the behaviour as troubling.

content.headline: Linda Cardellini embraces practical gore in Friday the 13th prequel
content.shortHeadline: Linda Cardellini enters the world of slasher horror
content.standfirst: In Crystal Lake, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original Friday the 13th killer. She describes the hands-on prosthetics behind the show’s bloodiest scenes and reflects on the long afterlife of Freaks and Geeks.

image.caption: Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees in Crystal Lake.

sources.originalTitle: ‘They pulled a guy’s face off. It’s my favourite bit!’ Linda Cardellini on Freaks and Geeks, Mad Men and slasher horror Crystal Lake

segments.body: Linda Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees in Crystal Lake, a prequel to the Friday the 13th films. She says one of the show’s most gruesome effects—a face pulled off with fishing wire—was created with practical prosthetics, and that seeing it happen helped shape her reaction.

segments.title: A career of unexpected turns
segments.body: Cardellini also looks back on Freaks and Geeks, cancelled before its first season had finished airing but later embraced as a lasting television favourite. After winning her first Emmy for DTF St Louis, she says she enjoys changing direction rather than committing to a “scream queen” identity.

content.headline: Aberfan survivors recall the long fight for justice in new documentary
content.shortHeadline: Aberfan’s families and their decades-long fight
content.standfirst: The documentary revisits the 1966 disaster and the failures that followed it, through the memories of survivors and bereaved families. Its review finds the treatment of the village by officials as distressing as the tragedy itself.

image.caption: The aftermath of the Aberfan disaster in 1966.

sources.originalTitle: Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back review – the contempt they have faced to get justice is sickening

segments.body: On 21 October 1966, a spoil tip engulfed a school and homes in Aberfan, killing 116 children and 28 adults. Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back begins with survivors’ and families’ memories before tracing the campaign to hold the National Coal Board and government to account.

segments.title: A second injury
segments.body: The documentary recounts how the inquiry blamed the Coal Board, yet no one was personally punished. Families also faced years of resistance over liability and the removal of the tips; the board demanded money from the disaster fund to pay for the work. The review highlights the village’s organising and the later return of the fund money by the Blair government.

content.headline: Seven shows to stream this week, from The Audacity to Lupin
content.shortHeadline: Seven shows to stream this week
content.standfirst: A new comedy about wealthy tech executives leads this week’s picks, alongside a killer-gnome series, a grooming documentary and new seasons of familiar streaming favourites.

image.caption: Billy Magnussen and Sarah Goldberg in The Audacity.

sources.originalTitle: The Audacity to Nobody Wants This: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Audacity, from Succession writer Jonathan Glatzer, sends up a rich, morally compromised tech CEO and the world around him. The guide says the comedy does not quite reach Succession’s heights, but finds plenty of bite in its portrait of people insulated by wealth.

segments.title: Other picks this week
segments.body: The week’s recommendations range from Australian horror-comedy Gnomes and a documentary about the online grooming and murder of Breck Bednar to returning series Nobody Wants This and Lupin. The selection also includes a Halloween edition of Last One Laughing and a three-part investigation into police access to the encrypted Sky ECC app.

content.headline: Tonight on TV: a ketamine documentary and rare Only Fools and Horses clips
content.shortHeadline: Tonight: ketamine, Only Fools and more
content.standfirst: Stacey Dooley meets long-term ketamine users, while Only Fools and Horses fans get a look at deleted scenes. The evening’s other picks include a family documentary and a Bafta-nominated film about addiction.

image.caption: Stacey Dooley in Down the K-Hole.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: Stacey Dooley learns about ‘ket bladder’

segments.body: Down the K-Hole follows Stacey Dooley as she speaks with long-term ketamine users about the effects of the drug, including bladder damage and the appeal of dissociation. The programme is presented as an eye-opening account of consequences, not as a first-hand investigation by Dooley into her own use.

segments.title: Other evening choices
segments.body: The schedule also offers previously unseen Only Fools and Horses clips, a documentary about a mother and daughter navigating addiction and estrangement, and a programme about novelist John le Carré. The guide rounds out its picks with baking, police drama and live sport.

content.headline: Time’s young offender institute drama shows how anger is reinforced
content.shortHeadline: Time examines anger inside a young offenders’ institute
content.standfirst: The third series of Jimmy McGovern’s prison drama follows boys held in near-isolation and the adults responsible for them. Its review finds a devastating account of violence, emotional need and a system that leaves little room for change.

image.caption: David Tennant and Louis McCartney in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time review – David Tennant’s furious drama is as important as Adolescence

segments.body: The final series of Time moves into a young offender institution where boys can be locked in their cells for 23 hours a day under a “keep apart” system. David Tennant plays a weary but not entirely unfeeling officer; Siobhan Finneran returns as a chaplain who has lost her faith but continues to work with the inmates.

perspectives.body: The review argues the series should receive the national attention given to Adolescence, while acknowledging that the prison system’s complexity and the bleakness of its subject may make that harder.

segments.title: What the drama makes visible
segments.body: The boys’ histories include serious violence, but the series also shows grief, abuse and a lack of language for emotion feeding further harm. The review praises the young cast and argues that the drama’s account of isolation and pent-up anger makes the realities of young offender institutions difficult to ignore.

content.headline: Sarah Solemani’s The Party brings class, grief and ambition to television
content.shortHeadline: Sarah Solemani on class, grief and The Party
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and showrunner discusses adapting Elizabeth Day’s novel into a drama about a journalist and a Tory politician, and how personal loss and class have shaped her work.

image.caption: Actor, writer and showrunner Sarah Solemani.

sources.originalTitle: Sarah Solemani: ‘I performed at my mum’s hospice bed two weeks before she died’

segments.body: Sarah Solemani stars in and runs The Party, adapted from Elizabeth Day’s novel. The drama follows a working-class journalist and a Conservative politician whose old friendship hides a secret. Solemani says she has long tried to bring stories about the British class system to television without being forced to treat class as a genre in itself.

segments.title: Writing from experience
segments.body: Solemani speaks about losing her mother at 16, the urgency that followed, and her view that creativity requires a willingness to be emotionally exposed. She also says the #MeToo movement changed working conditions on sets, describing a marked difference from her experience as a young actor.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic expedition into a strange, critical odyssey
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony is a strange Antarctic odyssey
content.standfirst: This exploration game sends a penguin through a world of Nazis, Lovecraftian horrors and scattered words. Its fractured storytelling becomes a critique of the human urge to conquer and plunder.

image.caption: A penguin explores the Antarctic world of Penguin Colony.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: Penguin Colony casts the player as a penguin exploring an Antarctic landscape where Nazis pursue an ancient entity. Words replace the usual treasure as collectibles, and hopping between different penguin species changes how the player moves through the terrain.

segments.title: A history seen from another angle
segments.body: The review praises the game’s unsettling shifts between low-poly exploration, narrated expedition history and archive footage. Its eventual critique of Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism is tied to a wider invitation to experience the world without treating it as something to conquer, though technical glitches occasionally interrupt the play.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time remake makes a classic feel new under the thumbs
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time gets a striking Switch 2 remake
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s remake updates movement, camera and sound for Switch 2 while preserving the game’s familiar world and puzzles. Link’s new look is divisive, but the preview finds a coherent reimagining in motion.

image.caption: Link in Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: The Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time gives Link a sprint, manual jump, free-rotating camera and a streamlined inventory. Familiar dungeons and puzzles remain, but the upgraded controls make the 1998 game feel markedly different to play.

perspectives.body: The preview sees Link’s glossy, wide-eyed redesign as a point of debate, but suggests its doll-like look may reflect a Japanese puppet-theatre tradition rather than a simple pursuit of 4K detail.

segments.title: The challenge of revisiting a classic
segments.body: The remake’s enhanced environments and newly orchestrated soundtrack help refresh the familiar adventure, though the reviewer questions whether Hyrule Field can recreate the freedom players felt in 1998. The more traditional dungeon structure may itself be part of the appeal for returning fans.

content.headline: Could a new wave of independent arcades bring gaming back to the high street?
content.shortHeadline: Independent arcades could bring gaming back to the high street
content.standfirst: After years of sprawling games designed to occupy players indefinitely, interest is growing in shorter experiences and social play. The case for independent arcades is less about nostalgia than shared discovery.

image.caption: Players return to the social experience of arcade gaming.

sources.originalTitle: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth

segments.body: The article argues that publishers’ pursuit of “forever games” has helped renew interest in shorter, more focused experiences. New arcade-minded titles and specialist venues suggest a possible return to gaming spaces where players can try different games without committing all their time to one.

segments.title: A local place for players
segments.body: Rather than simply reproducing retro bars, the model proposed is closer to an independent bookshop or record store: a curated collection, knowledgeable staff and events that help build a community. Arcade specialist Will Freeman sees small venues opening on that basis, though he cautions that the current signs do not amount to a boom.

perspectives.body: Freeman says gaming bars and cafés show that out-of-home gaming can be sustainable, but describes independent arcades as a handful of emerging projects rather than a boom.

content.headline: A £350 GTA collector’s box reflects gaming’s growing price barrier
content.shortHeadline: The £350 GTA box reflects gaming’s rising costs
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI merchandise box does not include the game itself. The article sees its price as part of a wider shift that risks making console and PC gaming feel like a luxury hobby.

image.caption: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI collector’s box.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s £350 Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection contains merchandise but no copy or download code for the game. With the game priced separately at £70, buying both would cost £420.

segments.title: Who can afford to play?
segments.body: The writer argues that expensive collector’s editions fit a broader pattern of rising console and game prices, as publishers pursue a smaller group of high-spending customers. Mobile games remain widely accessible, but the console and PC experiences that form the article’s focus are increasingly difficult to access without substantial spending.

content.headline: Japan’s spacecraft begins a five-year mission to bring back samples from Phobos
content.shortHeadline: Japan’s mission to bring back samples from Phobos
content.standfirst: The spacecraft is expected to reach Mars in 2027 and return to Earth in 2031 with material from the planet’s moon. Scientists hope the samples will help explain how Phobos and Deimos formed.

image.caption: Japan’s H3 rocket launches the spacecraft on its mission to Phobos.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Once-in-a-lifetime chance’: Japan launches historic mission to collect rocks from Mars’s moon Phobos

segments.body: Japan’s Martian Moons Exploration spacecraft has launched on a mission to collect and return samples from Phobos, one of Mars’s two small moons. The Japan-led project aims to bring at least 10 grams of material back to Earth in 2031.

segments.title: What scientists hope to learn
segments.body: The mission is designed to investigate whether Phobos and Deimos formed from debris after a major impact on Mars or were asteroids captured by the planet’s gravity. The spacecraft is due to reach the Mars region in August 2027, survey Phobos and attempt to collect samples before beginning its return journey.

content.headline: AI helps researchers trace 461 years of Britain’s maritime trading history
content.shortHeadline: AI helps map 461 years of maritime history
content.standfirst: Researchers used AI to process about 100,000 pages of handwritten records, uncovering patterns in trade and lost ports. The project offers a new way to explore historical archives at scale.

image.caption: Researchers used AI to analyse handwritten historical records.

sources.originalTitle: How AI revealed 400 years of seafaring history

segments.body: A University of Southampton project used AI to read around 100,000 pages of handwritten records at the National Archives, a task researchers say would have taken years by hand. The material covers 461 years, from the Elizabethan era to just before the Industrial Revolution.

segments.title: Trade, ports and surprising finds
segments.body: The records help map who traded what, and where. They suggest European markets accounted for around 80% of England’s recorded overseas trade in 1696–97, even as the British Empire expanded. The researchers also traced the disappearance of Ravenspurn, a once-thriving East Yorkshire port lost to coastal erosion.

content.headline: Orionid meteor shower peaks this week, but a bright Moon may hide many
content.shortHeadline: Orionids peak this week, with the Moon obscuring some meteors
content.standfirst: The annual shower is expected to peak on the night of 21–22 October. A bright Moon will make fainter meteors harder to see, though darker skies may follow after moonset.

image.caption: Chart showing the Orionids’ radiant near Orion.

sources.originalTitle: Starwatch: Catch the Orionid meteor shower streak across the night sky

segments.body: Earth’s passage through dust left by Halley’s comet brings the Orionid meteor shower, expected to peak during the night of 21–22 October. Under ideal conditions observers might see 10 to 20 meteors an hour, but the bright waxing Moon will drown out many of the fainter streaks.
The report advises finding a safe spot with a wide view of the sky and watching with the naked eye. Conditions should improve in the early hours after the Moon sets, when Orion is climbing higher.

content.headline: Google Cloud outage disrupts UK banks, services and court hearings
content.shortHeadline: Google Cloud outage disrupts banks and court hearings
content.standfirst: A power event at Google’s London cloud site affected banking services, delivery platforms and remote court hearings. Most services recovered during the day, but the incident renewed concerns about reliance on a small number of cloud providers.

image.caption: Revolut was among the services affected during the Google Cloud outage.

sources.originalTitle: Google says services recovering after cloud outage hits UK banks and websites
Google cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offline

segments.body: Google said a power event affected services at its London cloud operations on Tuesday. Customers reported problems with Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC, while Royal Mail, DPD and other services also appeared to be disrupted. Google said services were returning for most customers by the afternoon.

segments.title: Court access and cloud concentration
segments.body: The Guardian reported that the outage disrupted the remote-hearing video system used by courts in England and Wales, delaying several hearings. The Financial Conduct Authority said it was seeking more information from Google, in what the paper described as an early test of regulators’ new powers over critical cloud providers.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s reporting highlights consequences beyond consumer inconvenience: court proceedings were affected, and the outage is an early test of UK regulators’ oversight of cloud services used by financial firms.

segments.body: Google has not yet explained the cause of the power event, and said it would publish an analysis after its internal investigation. Revolut said customers’ money and data were safe; the BBC noted the company had not directly linked each affected service to the cloud outage.

content.headline: UK regulator proposes opening Apple’s contactless payment technology
content.shortHeadline: UK watchdog wants Apple to open up contactless payments
content.standfirst: The Competition and Markets Authority says Apple’s fees and restrictions may be limiting competition and wants rival apps to get access. Apple argues that opening the system could weaken privacy and security.

sources.originalTitle: UK asks Apple to widen access to its payment tech

segments.body: The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority is consulting on proposals that would require Apple to let more apps use the iPhone’s contactless payment technology.
